subject: bat
pitch: A fruit bat with its wings spread wide. A fluffy golden-brown body, a fox-like face with big dark eyes and a moist black nose, pointed ears, and leathery charcoal wings stretched between long finger bones with a small hooked claw on each thumb. It clutches a half-eaten fig in its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning the bat's pose—wings spread wide, clutching a fig in its feet—and deciding how to position it so the lowest points rest naturally rather than appearing to float.

Working out proportions and coordinates: body height, leg length down to the feet, and the fig's size and position so its bottom just touches ground level. Now I'm starting to lay out the skeleton hierarchy, beginning with the hips joint and the spine chain running from hips through chest to neck.

Adding head and jaw joints next, then sweeping the body along the spine chain with varying radii, considering countershaded fur coloring and maybe fluffy card details for texture.

Still building the head geometry...

Working out the ear spikes with pink inner accents, then starting to position the wing arm chains from shoulder to elbow with a spread, slightly raised pose.

Building out joint chains...

Mapping out the fan shape of fingers 2 through 5, each spreading from the wrist to different tip positions, then setting up three-joint chains per finger with a slight droop curve between wrist, mid, and tip.

Each finger gets a sweep with tapering radius and dark bone color, and now I'm planning the membrane connections — stretching skin between consecutive fingers with scalloped edges, plus a leading propatagium membrane from the arm to the second digit and a trailing membrane near the body.

Finishing edge B as a path from wrist to the hip area, letting the membrane resample it into a triangular skin shape even though it degenerates at the shared start point with edge A. Then I'm considering the propatagium between the arm and finger 2, but realizing the shoulder-to-wrist and wrist-to-tip edges differ too much in structure, so I'll skip that and think of another approach for connecting arm and fingers.

Defining the membrane triangles...

Now working out the leg rig from hip to foot with knee bend backward, parented to the hip joint, and positioning the feet to curl toes over the top of the clutched fig shape.

Still working out toe geometry...

Now I'm figuring out the fig's shape itself—thinking of it as a sphere with a bitten section revealing red flesh, considering whether to use a lathe geometry for the purple skin with a flat cut plane versus layering a full purple sphere with a front cutaway to keep things simpler.

Computing the wedge angle so the missing slice faces toward the viewer, around a 103-degree gap, and noting I'll need to handle the single-sided material so the interior doesn't look see-through from the back.

For the fig itself: a pinkish-red flesh sphere with a slightly smaller radius, scattered cream seed specks placed within the wedge opening, and a small stem — placing it toward the back-top so it doesn't collide with the clutching toes on top.

I'm using a mottled purple gradient paint for the fig's skin, attaching it via bone to the hips joint, and positioning the inner flesh and seeds along spherical coordinates within the wedge so the bite faces the camera.

For fluff, I'm scattering small lighter-gold cone shapes outward along the body surface normals to create a neck mantle and fuzzy texture, keeping the part count manageable. I'm also planning the body's coloring with a darker golden-brown back and paler belly, blending into a lighter gold near the neck for a natural countershaded bat look.

Now I'm working out the spine and limb proportions: a spine chain with a tapering radius array for the body and rump, a neck joint connecting to the head, extra fur cones near the neck for thickness, forward-pointing thumbs on each wrist, and a tapered radius sequence for the arm chain.

Checking wing and limb height alignment to make sure wingtips, toes, and ears stay within a sensible overall silhouette. I'm defining the hip and spine joints with catmull-rom spline points feeding into named spine segments, then attaching the arms off the chest joint with the shoulder offset slightly to one side.

Now I'm wiring up the head joint off the spine using a frame-based position like the neck example, with a slight forward/downward direction and local offsets for the muzzle. I'm also adding facial details—lighter snout fur, a gold-brown skull tone, and dark-edged ears with pink interiors—while keeping the total color palette compact.

Positioning the eyes and nose: placing eye spheres on the skull surface using local head coordinates, checking the geometry so they sit properly embedded, then adding small glossy highlight spheres offset toward the upper-forward side for a natural glint before moving on to the nose sphere at the snout tip.

Adding more capsule geometry...

For the jaw, I'm placing a joint bone with its own capsule mesh, keeping the mouth closed and neutral rather than adding an ajar pose or teeth details. I'll skip extra finger claws beyond the thumb to keep things simple.

Setting up the limb chains: arms use a catmull path through shoulder, elbow, and wrist, while fingers get a similar path with a slight upward bow at the midpoint and some droop at the tip, making sure the membrane between fingers shares the same starting point at the wrist and aligned edge directions.

Now I'm adding scalloped edges to the outer wing panels while keeping the inner ones smooth, mottling the membrane color by position, and giving it a thin double-sided thickness. I'm also writing a mirroring helper so left/right side coordinates can share the same vector definitions, then laying out wrist and finger/thumb points using that side multiplier.

Continuing the thumb and claw as bezier sweeps curving backward off the thumb tip...

I'm realizing I should pass the actual last joint in the arm's joint array as the parent rather than relying on a tip property that might not resolve correctly, then moving on to defining the membrane edges connecting the finger chains for the webbing surface.

The trailing edge connects tip5 to hip for a scalloped look, and I'm adding a propatagium patch near the thumb base, scattering fluff across the body surface with distance filtering, and placing a neck ruff along the surface sticks.

Now I'm setting up the color palette—gold, tan, dark brown, bone, and wing charcoal tones—plus a mottled paint treatment for the wings and body sweep, with varying radii along the spine chain for the body silhouette.
